correctness.rationale: For t1>t2>…>0 tending to zero, the telescoping map f(t_n)=sum_{j≥n}(t_j−t_{j+1})s_j is an isometric onto parametrization of Lip0(M,Y) by bounded adjacent slopes: every pairwise slope is a positive convex average of s_j. Under ratios t_{n+1}/t_n→0, either one adjacent slope attains the Lipschitz norm or a near-maximizing tail of slopes forces the fixed accumulation point 0 to norm f. Conversely, if the ratio limsup is positive, select sparse n_k with ratio≥δ and the next selected t-value at most δ t_{n_k}/2; attenuate an infinitely repeating ℓ∞ coordinate map by 1−1/(k+1). This realizes an isometric closed ℓ∞ subspace and yields uniform strict gap at p=0. At an isolated t_m, all finite adjacent-slope averages are individually below the norm, and the far-tail limit is below norm by the p=0 gap, so their supremum also stays below it. This completes the quantifiers for every nonzero real Banach target without extrapolating a finite test.
correctness.risk: Vector field scalar coefficients create one-dimensional span in Y; the theorem is only for real Banach spaces and the given ordered compact metric subset.

value.rationale: A sharp iff characterization for all compact sequences with one accumulation point, strengthened by an isometric closed ℓ∞ spaceability result on the complementary side for every Banach target, is a natural substantive classification problem in norm-attaining Lipschitz maps. It extends a notable named superlacunary example and separates pointwise from strong attainment.
value.risk: Does not classify arbitrary countable compact metric spaces or branching trees.

final_claim: For \(M=\{0\}\cup\{t_n\}\subset\mathbb R\) with strictly decreasing positive \(t_n	o0\), every Lipschitz map to any nonzero real Banach Y attains its pointwise Lipschitz norm iff \(t_{n+1}/t_n	o0\). Otherwise the pointwise nonattainers together with zero contain a closed isometric copy of \(\ell_\infty\), with an explicit uniform gap at zero.
limitations: Only a strictly decreasing convergent sequence with one accumulation point in a real line.
Targets are nonzero real Banach spaces.
Pointwise attainment differs from strong two-point attainment.
